Volume 05 · Chapter 06

Monopoly, oligopoly and pricing

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c05

By the endSolve market-power models and compare price and quantity competition.

Market power is a choice problem with a trading rule

Capability: solve market-power models and compare price and quantity competition. Prerequisite: General equilibrium and welfare. We also use economic cost and shutdown choices from firm choice, and the exact-surplus assumptions from competitive equilibrium. General game theory follows in Chapter 7; the few strategic concepts needed here are defined before use.

Two suppliers can charge marginal cost in one model and earn substantial markups in another. The difference can come from what they choose, when they choose it, how customers switch, and whether each can serve the whole market. Counting suppliers does not specify those mechanisms. We begin with a single seller, then change the pricing permissions and the competitive game.

All cases are original synthetic models. Q and qᵢ denote units sold during one period, p is dollars per unit, and profit, cost and surplus are dollars per period. Cost includes relevant opportunity costs. Demand coefficients carry the units needed for each equation; a coefficient of one is not permission to mix weekly quantities with annual costs. Product quality, available substitutes and the market's geographic and time boundaries are held fixed within each comparison.

Uniform-price monopoly: marginal revenue and global choice

A monopoly in the specified market is a single supplier facing the demand for that product and its outside alternatives. It has market power when its own choices affect the price or terms at which it sells. This does not give it freedom to choose an arbitrary price and arbitrary sales independently. Let inverse demand P(Q) be the price at which consumers buy Q, on a stated feasible range. A uniform-price seller receives the same per-unit price on every unit, so revenue and profit are

R(Q) = P(Q)Q,   π(Q) = P(Q)Q−C(Q).

For differentiable demand and cost at an interior positive output, marginal revenue is MR(Q) = P(Q)+QP′(Q) and marginal cost is MC(Q) = C′(Q). Selling an additional small amount earns P on the added units but reduces revenue on existing units by approximately −QP′. If P′ < 0, MR is below price. An interior optimum satisfies MR = MC, not P = MC.

The equality is a necessary local condition, not a global solution algorithm. Compare every feasible stationary point, kink, capacity boundary and zero-output alternative. Strict concavity of π on a convex feasible interval makes an interior stationary point the unique global optimum there. Continuity on a compact interval gives attainment; an unbounded choice set needs another existence argument. With an avoidable opening cost F, define C(0) = 0 and C(Q) = F+V(Q) for Q > 0, and compare the best operating contribution P(Q)Q−V(Q) with F. A cost already owed under both operating and shutdown alternatives cancels from their ranking.

For linear inverse demand P(Q) = a−bQ on 0 ≤ Q ≤ a/b, b > 0, and constant marginal cost 0 < c < a, operating contribution is (a−c)Q−bQ². Completing the square gives

(a−c)Q−bQ² = (a−c)²/(4b) − b[Q−(a−c)/(2b)]².

Thus QM = (a−c)/(2b) and pM = (a+c)/2 globally maximize contribution. A capacity K below QM changes the positive-output optimum to K. If c ≥ a and no subsidy or other benefit is present, positive sales cannot beat zero; if an opening fee is avoidable, the positive candidate must additionally cover it.

The Lerner condition and what its elasticity means

Suppose demand D(p) is differentiable and strictly decreasing locally, D(p) > 0 and p > 0, with a differentiable inverse P and a smooth, unconstrained positive monopoly optimum. Define the positive magnitude of demand elasticity ε = −D′(p)p/D(p) > 0. Since D′(p) = 1/P′(Q), the MR = MC equation implies

(p−MC)/p = −QP′(Q)/p = 1/ε.

The left side is the Lerner index, the marginal-cost markup as a fraction of price. It is not profit divided by revenue: fixed costs can absorb the operating contribution. With strictly positive MC, the interior condition requires ε > 1; with zero MC it gives ε = 1. Capacity constraints, discrete prices, kinks, multiproduct interactions, regulation and dynamic motives can invalidate this particular equality. The elasticity is the demand faced by this seller at the optimum under the specified alternatives, not an arbitrary correlation between observed prices and quantities.

Glenn Ellison's official MIT monopoly notes, slides 2–3, give the single-product MR and markup framework. Our global comparisons and boundary conditions determine when that local condition actually selects an output.

Transfers and forgone gains from trade

For the welfare calculations, assume quasilinear consumer preferences with sufficient numeraire, no externalities, fixed quality, truthful willingness to pay, and allocation to the highest-valued units. Gross benefit is B(Q) = ∫₀QP(s)ds. Consumer surplus is CS = B(Q)−pQ; variable producer surplus is pQ−V(Q); their sum is B(Q)−V(Q). Subtract avoidable real fixed costs when comparing activation or the number of plants. A common sunk cost cancels between current alternatives.

Under these assumptions an efficient quantity maximizes B(Q)−C(Q) over the same feasible possibilities. A smooth interior optimum has P(Q*) = MC(Q*), with a global justification still required. When monopoly restricts output below Q*, its deadweight loss is ∫QMQ*[P(s)−MC(s)]ds if the same fixed costs apply. Extra payments on units still traded transfer dollars from buyers to the seller; they do not themselves destroy that total. Distribution can nevertheless change substantially. Administrative expense, inefficient production, quality changes or expenditure to secure privileges can create additional real costs outside this simple triangle.

Worked example 1 — Price power, a markup and a surplus account

Take P(Q) = 90−Q and C(Q) = 18Q, with no fixed cost, on 0 ≤ Q ≤ 90. Contribution is 72Q−Q² = 1,296−(Q−36)². The unique monopoly choice is Q = 36, p = 54, revenue 1,944 and profit 1,296 dollars. MR = 90−2Q = 18, equal to MC. The elasticity magnitude at this point is 54/36 = 3/2, and (54−18)/54 = 2/3 = 1/ε.

Consumer surplus is (90−54)36/2 = 648. Total surplus is 648+1,296 = 1,944. Efficient output solves 90−Q = 18, giving Q* = 72 and total surplus (90−18)72/2 = 2,592. Monopoly therefore loses 648, the triangle (72−36)(54−18)/2.

At the marginal-cost benchmark consumers receive all 2,592 because variable profit is zero. Moving to monopoly lowers CS by 1,944: 1,296 is transferred to the producer and 648 is lost through unmade trades. Treating the entire consumer loss as deadweight loss would count the transfer incorrectly. These dollar sums implement the stated unweighted surplus criterion, not an interpersonal utility measurement or a Pareto ranking.

Pricing differently: information and enforceability matter

Price discrimination changes the terms offered across customers or units in ways not explained solely by corresponding cost differences. A delivery surcharge equal to additional delivery cost is not by itself evidence of discrimination. Three conventional labels describe different information and contracting assumptions.

First-degree, or perfect, discrimination lets the seller know each consumer's preferences and make enforceable personalized offers that extract all attainable surplus above the consumer's outside option. Assume no resale, sufficient ability to pay, no contracting cost and acceptance when indifferent. For a consumer with gross benefit Bᵢ(qᵢ) and outside surplus zero, a take-it-or-leave-it quantity/payment offer must satisfy Tᵢ ≤ Bᵢ(qᵢ). The seller sets Tᵢ = Bᵢ(qᵢ) and maximizes ΣᵢBᵢ(qᵢ)−C(Σᵢqᵢ). This is the same output/allocation objective as total surplus in this restricted environment. With constant marginal cost c, each interior served consumer has Bᵢ′(qᵢ) = c. All total surplus goes to the seller in the ideal extraction outcome, so efficiency does not mean buyers prefer it.

If customers reject exact indifference, extraction of every last dollar may be only a supremum: offer a small positive surplus to secure acceptance and recognize the resulting difference. Imperfect information, liquidity limits, unenforceable identity, resale and implementation costs can prevent the ideal allocation. A seller does not learn a customer's entire demand merely by announcing a personalized price.

Third-degree discrimination uses observable, enforceable groups and a separate uniform unit price within each. Let group g have inverse demand Pg(qg), with no cross-group demand effects or resale. Profit is ΣgPg(qg)qg−C(Σgqg). Smooth active groups satisfy MRg = MC at the same total output. With constant c and no group-specific fixed costs, group decisions separate; an unprofitable group can receive zero output. The interior rule becomes (pg−c)/pg = 1/εg. For common positive c this gives the higher price to the group with the smaller elasticity magnitude at the respective optimum. Income labels alone do not establish those elasticities.

Under a required common price p, instead maximize (p−c)ΣgDg(p), respecting every group's choke price, above which its demand is zero. Serving all groups cannot be assumed in advance. Allowing discrimination weakly increases maximum profit when the old uniform policy remains feasible and implementation is costless. It need not increase total surplus: output can change, and different marginal willingness to pay across groups can misallocate a fixed total quantity.

Second-degree discrimination offers a common menu, such as quantities and total charges, from which customers select. Private customer types must prefer their intended options and participation; the seller cannot simply attach a high price to a type it cannot observe. Information, signaling and selection develops those self-selection constraints, followed by contracts and incentives. This chapter's group-price calculation presumes verified groups and does not solve a hidden-type menu.

The information distinctions, personalized-offer benchmark and segmented-demand problem are developed in MIT's price-discrimination notes, slides 2–11. The following numbers and subsequent market-opening exercise independently exhibit different possible welfare directions.

Worked example 2 — Higher profit with unchanged output and lower welfare

A service has verified groups A and B, inverse demands PA = 50−qA and PB = 30−qB, and constant marginal cost 10. Demand is truncated at zero. There are no fixed costs, cross-group resale or other links between the demands.

With separate prices, each contribution is a concave quadratic. Group A maximizes 40qA−qA² = 400−(qA−20)²; B maximizes 20qB−qB² = 100−(qB−10)². Thus quantities are (20,10), prices (30,20), total quantity 30 and profit 500. Elasticities are 30/20 = 3/2 and 20/10 = 2, producing markups 2/3 and 1/2.

Find the global common-price alternative by branches. For 0 ≤ p ≤ 30, demand is 80−2p and profit is (p−10)(80−2p) = 450−2(p−25)², maximized at p = 25. Quantities are then (25,5), total 30. For 30 ≤ p ≤ 50 only A buys: profit is (p−10)(50−p) = 400−(p−30)², maximized at the boundary p = 30. At p ≥ 50 profit is zero. The global uniform optimum is therefore p = 25 with profit 450.

Pricing(qA,qB)CS in ACS in BProfitTotal surplus
Uniform(25,5)625/225/2450775
Separate group prices(20,10)20050500750

Since each inverse-demand slope is −1, each CS triangle is qg²/2. Discrimination raises profit by 50, lowers total CS by 75 and lowers total surplus by 25. Total output has not fallen; five units move from A to B. A's last purchased unit is valued at 30, while B's is valued at 20, so the allocation no longer equalizes marginal values across groups.

Efficient quantities at marginal value 10 are (40,20), giving total surplus 40²/2+20²/2 = 1,000. Uniform pricing loses 225; group pricing loses 250. Ideal first-degree discrimination could implement (40,20), charge total payments 1,200 to A and 400 to B, incur cost 600 and keep all 1,000 surplus as profit. The latter statement requires the personalized-contract and participation assumptions above; group membership alone does not permit it.

The minimum strategic language

An oligopoly has a small number of sellers whose choices affect one another's profits. To solve a model, specify each firm's allowed action, its profit for every action combination, information, timing and the customer-allocation rule. In a simultaneous model, each chooses without observing the other's current action; simultaneous describes information, not necessarily the same clock instant.

A best response is an action that maximizes a firm's profit holding the rival's action fixed. It can be a set. A Nash equilibrium is an action combination in which each action is a best response to the others. For two firms with actions a₁,a₂, this means πᵢ(aᵢ*,aⱼ*) ≥ πᵢ(aᵢ,aⱼ*) for every feasible unilateral deviation aᵢ. It is not a promise to cooperate, a claim of social efficiency or a claim that some adjustment process converges to it. Solving simultaneous first-order equations finds only candidates until the deviation inequalities are established.

Cournot: choose quantities and let the market clear

In the Cournot model, two firms choose quantities q₁,q₂ ≥ 0 simultaneously. The homogeneous product sells at P(Q), Q = q₁+q₂. Use P(Q) = max{a−bQ,0}, b > 0, and constant cost cqᵢ with 0 < c < a, no fixed or capacity constraint. The price floor completes the payoff definition even after excessive output.

Holding qⱼ fixed on the positive-price branch, firm i's profit is [a−c−bqⱼ]qᵢ−bqᵢ². The unique global best response is

BRᵢ(qⱼ) = max{0,(a−c−bqⱼ)/(2b)}.

When the linear coefficient is positive, completing the square proves the positive maximizer; when it is nonpositive, zero maximizes the branch. Any positive output on the zero-price branch makes a loss because c > 0, so it cannot overturn this comparison. The response reduces own output as rival output rises; it holds that rival output fixed rather than guessing that the rival will readjust during a deviation.

An equilibrium cannot have just one firm inactive: the active monopoly quantity would leave price above c, allowing the inactive firm a profitable small output. With both active, solve 2bq₁+bq₂ = a−c and bq₁+2bq₂ = a−c. Subtracting gives q₁ = q₂; hence

q₁* = q₂* = (a−c)/(3b),   QC = 2(a−c)/(3b),
pC = (a+2c)/3,   πᵢ = (a−c)²/(9b).

These intersecting unique best responses establish the equilibrium, including global deviations. If firms instead jointly maximize their summed profit, the joint-profit output is the monopoly output. An agreement to divide that output is not automatically an equilibrium: each may gain by expanding while the other keeps its agreed quantity. Such coordination is called a cartel in this model. Repeated interactions and enforcement change the strategic problem and are not assumed here.

For different positive costs c₁,c₂, replace c with cᵢ in the respective response. When both firms are active, solving gives q₁ = (a−2c₁+c₂)/(3b), q₂ = (a−2c₂+c₁)/(3b). If either is nonpositive, reconsider the zero-output branch; a negative calculated quantity is not a solution. At unequal costs, the same total Q can cost less if production is shifted to the cheaper firm with available capacity. Welfare analysis must then include productive allocation as well as the output gap.

Bertrand: choose prices with an explicit sales rule

Now change the actions. Two firms simultaneously choose nonnegative real-valued prices for an identical good, each has the same constant marginal cost c, and each can supply the entire market without a capacity constraint. Demand D(p) = max{(a−p)/b,0}, with 0 < c < a. Consumers know both prices, buy from the cheaper firm and split demand equally at a tie. There are no search or switching costs, no avoidable fixed participation costs, no repeated-game rewards, and no obligation to pay for goods not sold. A firm's profit is (pᵢ−c) times its allocated sales.

In this Bertrand model, (p₁,p₂) = (c,c) is a Nash equilibrium. Each earns zero. A unilateral higher price loses all customers and still earns zero; a lower price wins customers but sells at a loss. To prove uniqueness under these assumptions, exhaust the other cases:

  • If the minimum quoted price is below c, a firm selling there makes a loss and can instead quote above the rival and sell zero.
  • If one charges c and the other more, the lower-price firm can raise its quote to a price strictly between c and min{the rival's price,a}, retaining positive sales at a positive margin.
  • If the lower price lies strictly between c and a and prices differ, the currently unsupplied firm can undercut it slightly, stay above c and gain positive profit. If prices tie there, a small undercut wins the whole market instead of half; continuity of positive demand makes a sufficiently small undercut profitable.
  • If both prices are at least a, both sell zero, and a quote strictly between c and a yields positive profit.

This proof uses the ability to undercut by arbitrarily small amounts, the same product and cost, and the capacity to meet all diverted demand. With a discrete price grid, a binding capacity, differentiation, unequal costs or another tie/rationing rule, solve the altered deviation problem. For example, a constrained low-price seller may leave customers whom a higher-price seller can profitably serve. An asymmetric-cost result cannot be imported without its tie rule.

The Cournot and Bertrand benchmarks and the role of differentiation are presented in MIT's static-competition notes, slides 2–7. Our derivations specify the complete action/payoff domains and the equal-split, equal-cost case; they do not adopt the notes' separate asymmetric-cost allocation convention.

Worked example 3 — The same demand and cost, different games

Return to demand P(Q) = max{90−Q,0} and cost 18 per unit. In Cournot, BRᵢ(qⱼ) = max{0,(72−qⱼ)/2}; the intersection is (24,24). At the rival's 24, own profit on the positive-price branch is 48q−q² = 576−(q−24)². Larger output reaching zero price earns negative profit. This certifies no profitable deviation over the entire nonnegative quantity domain.

Total output is 48, price 42, and each firm's profit is (42−18)24 = 576. CS = 48²/2 = 1,152; total surplus is 1,152+1,152 = 2,304, so DWL = 2,592−2,304 = 288. In the continuous-price Bertrand version, both quote 18, total demand is 72, each sells 36 under the tie rule and both earn zero. CS and total surplus are 2,592.

Specified modelTotal quantityPriceTotal profitCSDWL
Uniform monopoly36541,296648648
Cournot duopoly48421,1521,152288
Unconstrained Bertrand duopoly721802,5920

The two duopoly rows have the same number of firms. In one, a deviation keeps the rival's quantity fixed; in the other, a small price cut can capture all its customers. The resulting ranking is a conclusion for these common primitives and rules, not a universal ranking of every industry labeled monopoly or oligopoly.

Entry, fixed costs and the boundaries of a market

An incumbent's current profit is not an entrant's expected profit. Entry can change prices, quantities and customers' alternatives. Evaluate an entry investment against the operating profit expected after entry, over a horizon consistent with the cost. A one-time investment cannot be compared directly with an annual profit without discounting and a time horizon. Once irrevocably paid, it is sunk in the subsequent pricing or quantity decision.

Here an entry barrier means an obstacle that limits the ability of potential rivals to enter and compete. Identify the mechanism rather than infer it from incumbent profit: exclusive access to an essential input, an enforceable exclusive right, switching costs, the difficulty of assembling compatible users, or scale and financing requirements may matter. Some are real resource costs, some confer an incumbent-specific advantage, and their welfare implications differ. A fixed cost shared by every potential firm can limit viable entry without proving that an incumbent engaged in exclusion.

A natural monopoly at a stated output range is a technology for which a single supplier can produce total output more cheaply than splitting it among suppliers. For identical technologies C(q) = F+cq at q > 0, with C(0) = 0 and F > 0, any division into n positive plants costs nF+cQ instead of F+cQ. The extra (n−1)F is real duplication in this model. Yet an unconstrained monopoly may restrict Q. Charging only c would fail to recover the single plant's avoidable F. Efficient scale, financing, incentive design and the chosen welfare criterion are separate questions; the cost comparison alone does not establish an optimal regulatory policy.

MIT's entry notes, slides 2–8, separate entry costs from profits in the subsequent competition model and from the welfare effect of entry. We use that timing distinction in a one-entrant exercise; the notes' general entry and dynamic-learning models are beyond this chapter.

Finally, market definition is substantive. A supplier may be unique in one narrow product label but face close substitutes, imports or a different delivery channel. Differentiation can retain customers after a small price increase; the all-or-nothing Bertrand allocation then fails. Estimates need evidence about substitution, marginal costs, capacity, quality, customer information, timing and feasible entry. Neither a firm count nor a price–average-cost gap identifies a monopoly elasticity, an equilibrium concept, collusion or a welfare loss.

Exercises

  1. For P(Q) = 70−2Q on 0 ≤ Q ≤ 35 and C(Q) = 10Q+Q², derive the global uniform monopoly output, price, profit and CS. Find efficient output and DWL under the chapter's surplus assumptions, and verify the Lerner identity. Then impose capacity Q ≤ 8. Solve again, calculate MR−MC and explain why the unconstrained markup equality need not hold. Use the same capacity constraint when identifying the feasible efficient benchmark.
  2. In Worked example 1, add an avoidable opening cost F, with shutdown cost zero. Give the optimal output set at F = 1,296 and at F = 1,300. If the 1,300 has instead already been paid irreversibly, give output, operating profit including that cost and shutdown profit. For the avoidable-cost case, calculate total surplus at Q = 72 after paying F = 1,300 and explain why positive feasible surplus alone does not make uniform-price operation privately profitable.
  3. Four identifiable consumers can each buy at most one indivisible unit, with dollar values 52,41,29,17. Marginal cost is 20, no fixed cost applies, and a consumer buys when indifferent. Compare the optimal nonnegative uniform price with ideal first-degree discrimination: calculate quantity, revenue, profit, CS and DWL. Justify your global price search. State the information, enforceability and participation assumptions needed for full extraction.
  4. There are verified, non-reselling groups with inverse demands PA = 80−qA and PB = 20−qB, each truncated at zero, and marginal cost 10. Solve globally for a common price by demand branches, then solve for separate group prices. Calculate quantities, profits, CS and total surplus in both cases. Compare the welfare direction with Worked example 2 and identify the mechanism.
  5. Two Cournot firms face P(Q) = max{84−Q,0}, with marginal costs c₁ = 12 and c₂ = 30. Derive and check both best responses, solve the equilibrium, and calculate profits, CS and total surplus. If production can be freely assigned to the cheaper firm with unlimited capacity, find the efficient benchmark and decompose the welfare gap into an output loss and an extra production-cost loss. Re-solve the equilibrium when c₂ becomes 54; reject any negative-output candidate explicitly.
  6. Under the primitives of Worked example 3, firms propose q₁ = q₂ = 18 to share monopoly output. Find each proposed profit and one firm's globally optimal deviation holding the rival at 18; is the agreement a Nash equilibrium? In the continuous-price game, show numerically why a tie at price 30 is not an equilibrium. Finally impose capacity 30 per firm. Under efficient rationing, the cheaper firm serves the highest-value willing buyers first, so a higher-price firm has residual demand max{D(phigh)−30,0} when the cheaper plant is full. Test the proposed price pair (18,18) using a deviation to 19. Do not claim to have solved the entire capacity game.
  7. In Worked example 3's market, one incumbent faces one possible entrant. Entry costs F now, is irreversible, and leads to the stated Cournot equilibrium in the only subsequent operating period; assume no discounting within this horizon, and staying out yields zero. Determine entry when F = 700 and when F = 500, and compare with an argument based on the incumbent's monopoly profit. Separately, for technology C(q) = 400+18q at positive q and zero when inactive, compare the resource cost of supplying Q = 60 with one versus two positive-output plants. What does marginal-cost pricing recover, and which conclusions about welfare or exclusion do these calculations leave open?
  8. A market has D(p) = max{14−p,0}, two homogeneous unlimited-capacity sellers, cost 2 per unit and equal splitting at a price tie. Unlike the baseline, each permitted quote is an integer dollar amount from 0 to 14. Prove that (3,3) is a Nash equilibrium by covering every feasible unilateral deviation. Give a profitable deviation if continuous prices are restored. Evaluate the claim “two firms and a positive markup prove collusion,” identifying further evidence that would be needed in an actual market.
Complete solutions and interpretation

  1. Profit is (70−2Q)Q−10Q−Q² = 60Q−3Q² = 300−3(Q−10)². The unique unconstrained monopoly choice is Q = 10, p = 50 and profit 300; CS = (70−50)10/2 = 100. MC = 10+2Q and MR = 70−4Q both equal 30 there. Efficient surplus is ∫₀Q(70−2s)ds−10Q−Q² = 60Q−2Q² = 450−2(Q−15)², maximized at Q = 15. Monopoly surplus is 400, so DWL = 50. Equivalently integrate 60−4Q from 10 to 15.

    Direct demand is (70−p)/2, so ε = (1/2)50/10 = 5/2 and (50−30)/50 = 2/5 = 1/ε. With capacity 8, profit is increasing throughout the feasible interval and reaches 288 at Q = 8, p = 54. CS = 8² = 64 and total surplus is 352. MR = 38, MC = 26, so MR−MC = 12 > 0: profitable marginal expansion is infeasible. The actual markup is 28/54 = 14/27, whereas 1/ε = 16/54 = 8/27. The same capacity limits the efficient benchmark to Q = 8, with the same 352 surplus and zero output distortion relative to that feasible benchmark. Comparing instead with unconstrained surplus 450 includes the capacity restriction's 98-dollar loss.

  2. Maximum operating contribution is 1,296 at Q = 36. At F = 1,296, both Q = 0 and Q = 36 give zero profit; every other positive quantity does worse. At avoidable F = 1,300 choose Q = 0: Q = 36 would lose 4. If 1,300 is already unavoidable, choose Q = 36, earning 1,296−1,300 = −4 rather than the shutdown loss −1,300. The incremental benefit of operating is still 1,296.

    At efficient Q = 72, gross net variable surplus is 2,592; after the avoidable setup it is 1,292 > 0. A uniform-price seller cannot collect all of that surplus and would recover at most 1,296 of the 1,300 setup cost. Feasible gains from trade and the revenue collectable under a particular tariff differ. Under the ideal first-degree assumptions, full extraction could cover setup and leave profit 1,292, but that is a different permitted pricing mechanism.

  3. For uniform pricing it suffices to check reservation values and the zero-sales option: between adjacent values quantity is constant, so increasing price to the next accepted reservation value raises profit. Prices 52,41,29,17 yield quantities 1,2,3,4 and profits 32,42,27,−12. No sales gives zero. The optimum is p = 41, Q = 2, revenue 82, cost 40 and profit 42. CS is 52−41 = 11, so total surplus is 53.

    Efficient trade serves values 52,41,29, since each exceeds cost 20, and excludes 17. Total surplus is 32+21+9 = 62. Uniform pricing therefore has DWL 9. Ideal personalized charges 52,41,29 yield Q = 3, revenue 122, cost 60, profit 62 and CS zero, with DWL zero. This requires known individual values, preventable resale and impersonation, enforceable offers, ability to pay and the stipulated acceptance at indifference. With strict-surplus participation, small price reductions approach but do not attain all 62 as profit.

  4. For 0 ≤ p ≤ 20, common-price demand is 100−2p and profit is (p−10)(100−2p). Its derivative is 120−4p > 0 throughout this branch, so its maximum is 600 at p = 20. For 20 ≤ p ≤ 80, only A buys; profit is (p−10)(80−p) = 1,225−(p−45)², maximized at p = 45. Prices at least 80 give zero profit. Thus the global uniform optimum has p = 45, (qA,qB) = (35,0), profit 1,225, CS = 35²/2 = 1,225/2 and total surplus 3,675/2 = 1,837.5.

    Discrimination leaves A at q = 35,p = 45 and opens B at q = (20−10)/2 = 5,p = 15. Total quantity becomes 40, profit 1,250, CS = (35²+5²)/2 = 625 and total surplus 1,875. The gains are 25 profit, 25/2 CS and 75/2 total surplus. Unlike Worked example 2, a previously excluded group trades and A's allocation is unchanged. Neither a universal benefit nor a universal harm from third-degree discrimination follows. The solution needs the no-resale and group-verification assumptions; otherwise the separate prices need not be implementable.

  5. The best responses are max{0,(72−q₂)/2} and max{0,(54−q₁)/2}. Solving 2q₁+q₂ = 72 and q₁+2q₂ = 54 gives (q₁,q₂) = (30,12), Q = 42 and p = 42. Each is a global response: given q₂ = 12, firm 1 has profit 60q₁−q₁² = 900−(q₁−30)² on the positive-price branch; given q₁ = 30, firm 2 has 24q₂−q₂² = 144−(q₂−12)². Zero-price positive output gives losses. Profits are 900 and 144; CS = 42²/2 = 882; total surplus is 1,926.

    With all production at cost 12, efficient Q = 84−12 = 72 and surplus is 72²/2 = 2,592. At the actual Q = 42 but all production assigned to firm 1, surplus would be 72(42)−42²/2 = 2,142. The output gap loses 2,592−2,142 = 450 = (72−42)²/2. Actual use of the higher-cost plant wastes an additional (30−12)12 = 216. Total gap is 666 = 450+216.

    At c₂ = 54 the interior formulas give q₂ = (84−108+12)/3 = −4 and q₁ = 40, so reject that branch. Set q₂ = 0; firm 1's best response is 36. At that quantity, firm 2's response is max{0,(84−54−36)/2} = 0. The equilibrium is (36,0), price 48 and profits (1,296,0). Firm 2's positive-output marginal profit at zero is −6, consistent with remaining inactive.

  6. At (18,18), price is 54 and each profit is (54−18)18 = 648. Holding the rival at 18, the best response is (72−18)/2 = 27. Its profit is 54q−q² = 729−(q−27)², so the deviation earns 729, a gain of 81. The joint-profit allocation is not a one-period Nash equilibrium.

    In the continuous-price game, a tie at 30 splits demand 60 equally, giving each profit (30−18)30 = 360. A quote 29 wins all 61 units and earns (29−18)61 = 671. The tie therefore fails the deviation test.

    With capacities 30, at (18,18) total demand 72 exceeds total capacity 60; both sell 30 and earn zero. Raise one price to 19. The other plant remains full at 30. Under the specified efficient rationing, residual demand is D(19)−30 = 71−30 = 41, exceeding the deviator's capacity. It sells 30 at a one-dollar margin, earning 30. Thus (18,18) is not an equilibrium in this capacity game. This profitable deviation disproves that candidate; it neither establishes the new equilibrium nor claims that every rationing rule produces the same outcome.

  7. After entry the entrant earns the Cournot operating profit 576. Entry at F = 700 gives −124, so it stays out; at F = 500 it earns 76 net and enters. The relevant opportunity is not the incumbent's monopoly profit 1,296, because that monopoly configuration ends when the entrant competes. These are one-period investment comparisons with the subsequent game specified; uncertain future profits or multiple periods require a different calculation.

    At total output 60, one plant costs 400+18(60) = 1,480. Two positive plants cost 800+18(60) = 1,880 regardless of the output split, so duplication costs 400. Pricing at marginal cost 18 raises only 1,080 and leaves the single plant's setup cost uncovered by 400. The cost calculation supports a natural-monopoly property over this technology, not a conclusion that unrestricted monopoly pricing maximizes welfare. Demand distortions, financing and regulation remain to be analyzed. A real resource cost facing all entrants also does not by itself establish strategic exclusion or an incumbent-specific privilege.

  8. At (3,3), demand is 11, each sells 11/2 and earns 11/2 = 5.5. An integer deviation to 0 or 1 wins demand at a negative margin; a deviation to 2 earns zero; any allowed integer from 4 through 14 sells nothing and earns zero. The only remaining action is 3 itself. Therefore no feasible unilateral deviation improves profit, proving Nash equilibrium on the finite price grid.

    With continuous quotes, 2.9 wins 11.1 units at a 0.9-dollar margin, earning 9.99 > 5.5. The discrete equilibrium fails once the missing deviations become feasible. Hence two firms with a positive markup do not prove collusion. The observation can be consistent with the explicitly noncooperative grid model. An empirical assessment would need evidence about permitted price increments, product substitution/quality, costs at the margin rather than average cost, capacity, search or switching frictions, timing and conduct. Naming several possible mechanisms does not identify which one actually generated observed prices.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain why the monopolist lowers revenue on existing units when it expands, why buyer losses include a transfer as well as deadweight loss, and why third-degree discrimination is not perfect discrimination. Then compare a Cournot deviation with a Bertrand deviation while explicitly holding the rival's chosen action fixed. A successful explanation states the assumptions that permit a tiny price cut to capture an entire market.

Delayed check: for P(Q) = max{66−Q,0}, constant marginal cost 6 and no fixed costs, reconstruct monopoly, symmetric Cournot duopoly and continuous-price Bertrand outcomes. Give price, total quantity, each firm's profit where applicable and DWL under the chapter's surplus assumptions. Identify one altered trading rule that invalidates the Bertrand conclusion.

Delayed-check answer

Efficient output is 60 and total surplus 1,800. Monopoly chooses Q = 30,p = 36, profit 900, CS 450 and DWL 450. Cournot chooses q₁ = q₂ = 20, Q = 40,p = 26; each profit is 400, CS is 800 and DWL is 200. Bertrand has p₁ = p₂ = 6, Q = 60 split equally, both profits zero, CS 1,800 and DWL zero. A binding capacity with a specified residual-demand rule, or a discrete price grid excluding arbitrarily small cuts, requires a new deviation analysis.

Further study and scope

The source slides provide primary methods; all cases and exercises here are original. We solved one-product static pricing and explicit two-firm games. We have not estimated real conduct, evaluated a current legal rule or proved that all market structures have pure equilibria. Multiproduct pricing, differentiated demand estimation, dynamic competition and general capacity-constrained price equilibria require further models. Next, Game theory and strategic behavior develops dominance, mixed strategies, sequential decisions and credible commitment.

Sources and further study

  • Glenn Ellison, MIT 14.271: Lecture 1, Monopoly Pricing and Durable Goods, Part I (Fall 2022) — Single-product monopoly profit, MR=MC and the Lerner elasticity condition; conventional deadweight-loss versus profit/consumer-surplus distinction. The chapter supplies its own global and activation comparisons.
  • Glenn Ellison, MIT 14.271: Lecture 3, Price Discrimination, Part 1 (Fall 2022) — First-, second- and third-degree information distinctions; personalized take-it-or-leave-it offers, resale and observability constraints; segmented uniform pricing and quantity/allocation channels in welfare.
  • Glenn Ellison, MIT 14.271: Lecture 5, Static Competition and Models of Differentiation, Part 1 (Fall 2022) — Cournot quantity choice, residual-profit condition and cost-allocation caveat; homogeneous-good Bertrand benchmark and the importance of differentiation, capacity, information and timing assumptions.
  • Glenn Ellison, MIT 14.271: Lecture 16, Entry (Fall 2022) — Entry investment versus profits in the subsequent competition model, and the distinction between private entry incentives and the full consumer/producer/fixed-cost welfare account.
